sections.html:
The 2020 census counted 125,447 people and 58,648 housing units in Cochise County. Vacant units made up 13.1% of the stock, and 68.8% of occupied homes were lived in by their owners. Sierra Vista is the biggest city. Douglas, Bisbee, Benson, Willcox and Tombstone are also cities, while many houses stand in unincorporated spots like Whetstone, St. David, Elfrida and Palominas. A rural parcel out there can behave quite differently at sale time from a lot in town.

Fort Huachuca, the Army post at Sierra Vista, means some owners must sell on the schedule of a transfer order. Median age is 44.0 years and 24.2% of residents are 65 or older, so a good share of listings follow a death or a move toward family. Those houses often carry a tax bill no one has opened for months.

Two county desks touch every parcel. The Assessor assigns a value, and the Treasurer mails the bill and receives payment. A pending sale means a call to the Treasurer for a payoff number, while a dispute about value belongs with the Assessor.

The rest of this page follows the Arizona statutes behind both offices and links to each one.

A year of real property tax in Arizona is paid in two pieces. One is due October 1, the other March 1, and they turn late at 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1 respectively (A.R.S. 42-18052).

PaymentDue dateCounts as late
First half of the billOctober 1November 1, at 5:00 p.m.
Second half of the billMarch 1May 1, at 5:00 p.m.
Whole bill of $100 or lessOctober 1, paid in one pieceDecember 31, at 5:00 p.m.

Should a cutoff land on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, it rolls to the next business day. If the first half is still open on your account, interest is already building, as described next.

The charge on a late bill is 16 percent a year, not compounded, counted from the day the bill turned delinquent. Start a month by one day and you pay for all of it (A.R.S. 42-18053). Every month a late first half sits unpaid adds to the cost.

Three situations switch interest off:

  • A county office, either the assessor or the treasurer, caused the problem by making an error.
  • You clear the entire year's bill by December 31, even if the first half arrived late.
  • A mortgage or deed of trust on the parcel was released the year before, and the supervisors approve a one-time waiver per property.

The middle item matters most to sellers. If November 1 came and went without a payment, paying the whole year before December 31 can wipe the interest out, which is cheaper than finding it on the closing statement.

sections.h2: The tax lien and your sale
sections.html:
Each January 1 the county's claim for that year's tax attaches to the house. Almost every other lien ranks below it, with state liens and tax liens from other years as the exceptions (A.R.S. 42-17153).

It goes away only three ways: everything owed is paid, a buyer takes title at a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. Because of that, the buyer's title company checks the balance with the Treasurer and wants it settled by closing.

Heirs of someone who stopped paying and landlords who ignored a bill after a tenant left run into this most. The debt stays attached to the house, so the sale proceeds cover it.

Back taxes slow a sale down but rarely stop it. Here is how it usually goes:

  1. The Treasurer gives you, or your title company, the balance through the date you plan to close.
  2. You find out which pieces are open: a current half, both halves, or older years.
  3. Escrow lists the payoff on the settlement statement.
  4. At the table, the payoff comes out of your proceeds and the lien is released.

A cash buyer taking the house as-is still needs the lien cleared, yet there is no appraisal or underwriting calendar to wait on, which may shorten the time to the table.

Each year the assessor mails owners of record a notice listing full cash value, and limited property value where it applies, ahead of March 1 (A.R.S. 42-15101). A person buying through a deed of trust or sale agreement gets a copy too.

Think the figure is too high? Petition the assessor within 60 days of the mailing date, with the postmark counting as your filing date (A.R.S. 42-16051). Say what you believe the value is and how you arrived at it. Under the market approach, include a comparable property or your own sale.

After an owner dies and the house passes by beneficiary deed, notices still go to the old address. The beneficiary has to write to the assessor with a certified death certificate and a new address. Do that soon, because an unseen notice can run out the 60 days.

sections.h2: A tax year from the seller's seat
sections.html:
Reading the calendar from a seller's point of view helps you time a listing. The lien for a given year starts on January 1. The Assessor's notice arrives by March 1, and your 60-day appeal clock starts when it is mailed. Bills follow in the fall, with the first half due October 1 and a safe zone to avoid interest closing on December 31. The second half comes due March 1 and turns late after May 1.

If you close in the spring, expect escrow to ask which halves are paid. A house that closes in December gives you the chance to clear the whole year in one payment and remove any interest worry before the new owner takes over.

sections.h2: What to gather before you call the Treasurer
sections.html:
Keep your parcel number and the owner name as it appears on the bill handy. Old bills in a drawer, mail forwarded from an estate, and notices sent to a former address are all common in this county, where many owners live somewhere else for part of the year. If you cannot find a bill, call and ask for the balance rather than waiting for one to show up, since a missing statement never wipes out the tax.

Ask for three things on the same call: the amount due today, the amount due on the day you expect to close, and whether any older years are still open. Write down the date and the figures and pass them to your title company so everyone is working from the same number.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for the spring half of the Cochise County bill?
faqs.a: Pay by 5:00 p.m. on May 1 to stay current. The half itself is due March 1, and a weekend or holiday moves the cutoff to the following business day.

faqs.q: How is a late Cochise County bill charged?
faqs.a: Sixteen percent a year, simple, counted by the month with a partial month rounded up. Clearing the entire year before December 31 means no interest is collected.

faqs.q: Will unpaid tax block me from selling a house in Cochise County?
faqs.a: No. The tax is a lien, and escrow pays it from your proceeds at closing after the Treasurer supplies the balance.

faqs.q: How much time do I have to contest the assessed value?
faqs.a: Sixty days from the day the assessor mailed your notice. The postmark is treated as your filing date.

faqs.q: When does the tax lien start on a Cochise County home?
faqs.a: January 1 of the tax year. It lasts until the bill is paid, a buyer takes title at a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued.
